problem: RunState.Tick guards dt with `if (dt < 0f) throw`, but its own error message states the invariant as "dt must be >= 0." Those are not the same predicate. float.NaN < 0f is false, so Tick(float.NaN) passes a guard whose stated contract NaN violates (NaN >= 0f is also false), and float.PositiveInfinity passes it too. The call then executes `ElapsedSeconds += dt`. Because NaN is absorbing under addition, a single Tick(NaN) makes ElapsedSeconds permanently NaN for the rest of the run: every later Tick with a valid dt leaves it NaN, and only Reset clears it. Infinity behaves the same way, saturating ElapsedSeconds to +Infinity irrecoverably. The failure is silent -- no exception, no flag, IsOver stays false, TickCount keeps counting correctly -- so a run continues to look healthy while its clock is destroyed, and every downstream comparison against ElapsedSeconds (a wave timer, a survival threshold, a difficulty ramp) silently takes the false branch, since all comparisons with NaN are false. This is exactly the class of defect WO-0007's seed/tick coordinate exists to make reportable, and it is the one thing the coordinate cannot report, because TickCount would read as correct. WO-0007's twelve criteria do not cover it: criterion 4 only obliges dt < 0 to throw, criterion 3 obliges any non-throwing Tick to increment, and criterion 11 preserves pre-existing validation, so the implementation satisfies the specification as written. The specification is what is incomplete. Worse, the independent verification did not merely miss this -- it ratified it. Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/RunStateVerificationTests.cs:132-139 asserts that Tick(float.NaN) is accepted and increments, with the comment "NaN < 0 is always false, so NaN passes the dt < 0 check", which reads the implementation's behaviour back as the requirement. Neither that test nor Criterion3_PositiveInfinityDtIncrements nor Criterion3_ManyTicksWithVariedDt ever asserts anything about ElapsedSeconds after the poisoning tick, so the poisoned state is invisible to a green suite. There is currently a passing test locking this defect in.

proposedWork: A follow-up L3 work order to engineering, scoped to Assets/Core/Run/** and Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/**, that does three things. First, amend WO-0007's contract with an additional acceptance criterion authored by the work-order author, not by the implementer: Tick(dt) must reject every dt that is not a finite non-negative number, so that float.NaN, float.PositiveInfinity and float.NegativeInfinity all throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException and none of them increments TickCount or changes ElapsedSeconds; and ElapsedSeconds must be finite after any sequence of non-throwing Tick calls with finite dt. Second, change the guard in RunState.Tick from `dt < 0f` to a predicate that actually expresses the documented invariant -- rejecting anything for which `dt >= 0f` is false, which catches NaN, plus an explicit infinity rejection -- so the code and its own error message agree. Third, and this is the part that needs an explicit ruling rather than quiet action: the fix inverts what three currently-passing tests assert. Criterion3_NaNDtIncrements and Criterion3_PositiveInfinityDtIncrements must be replaced by tests asserting that Tick throws and leaves TickCount and ElapsedSeconds untouched, and Criterion3_ManyTicksWithVariedDt must drop its non-finite entries into their own throwing cases. That is a specification correction being applied to tests that encoded the defect, and it must be authorised as such in the work order, because an implementer who edits those assertions without that authorisation is indistinguishable from one weakening a test to go green. Add a regression test that ticks NaN and then asserts ElapsedSeconds is finite -- it fails today and passes after the change.
expectedBenefit: Removes a silent, absorbing corruption of the run clock that no exception, flag or currently-passing test reveals, and that defeats the seed-plus-tick bug coordinate WO-0007 was built to provide, since TickCount reads as correct while ElapsedSeconds is NaN. Also retires a green test that presently certifies the defect as intended behaviour, which is the more expensive problem: as it stands, the next agent to read RunStateVerificationTests.cs will conclude that accepting NaN is a requirement.
